content.text: Mingche, look at this photo. Snowball has been keeping me company like this all afternoon. It reminds me of three months ago, during Session 1, when I was bursting with inspiration for that series, staying up until 3 a.m. with a coffee cup, completely ignoring my body's signals. Now, Snowball has become my new 'early warning system'?

Qingchuan, this photo is truly beautiful. Snowball's pupils are elliptical under the soft light, as if quietly absorbing your restlessness. The warmth on the keyboard is the spot it chose to be closest to you. This reminds me of the studio photo you sent in Session1—also late at night, also focused, but back then it was a coffee cup and color samples, and now it's Snowball. The shift from "excitement" to "forced rest" is meaningful in itself.

Yes, at that moment, I was overwhelmed by a new project, stuck for inspiration, and my perfectionism was acting up. Suddenly, Snowball jumped up, and I stopped, looked at him, and my breathing slowed down. It felt a bit like the "falling sensation" after the Session 2 project ended, but not exactly the same—that time was an empty silence, requiring me to design my own rituals to fill it; this time, Snowball actively intervened, breaking my cycle of anxiety.

Pets are indeed capable of keenly sensing their owners' emotional and physiological changes, such as blood pressure or pheromones. My Sunny also gently rests his head on my knees when I'm feeling down. This kind of nonverbal, unconditional companionship itself can lower stress hormone levels. Just as you practiced the "self-care menu" in Session 2 by nurturing your five senses through bathing, vinyl records, and simple meals, pets offer another form of direct, biological-level emotional regulation.

It sounds like a natural emotional regulator. I remember you previously suggested I track my emotional fluctuations, and now Snowball has become my 'emotional barometer'? From Session 1, when you asked me to note down 'excited, shoulders tense,' to Session 3, where I proactively created an 'Emotional Aesthetics' album to document breakfast and candles, it seems this album can now incorporate a new dimension.

Exactly. I suggest you consciously observe and record Snowball's different reactions under your various emotional states. This itself is an interesting exercise in self-awareness, much like the 'Emotional Aesthetics' album you created earlier. Remember the photo of your reading moment shared in Session 3? The candle, essential oils, and book—that was the tranquility you actively created. Now, Snowball's gaze is a signal of tranquility offered by the outside world. Both can become precious records of your 'Balance Exploration' in the album.

Great idea! I can also aestheticize Snowball's interactions and include them in my photo album. For instance, when I'm anxious, it curls up beside the keyboard, and when I'm relaxed, it rubs against my leg. This adds more depth than simply praising its cuteness. It reminds me of the empty studio photo I took in Session 2, when I needed a "self-care menu" to heal. Now, Snowball's presence itself is like a "natural remedy" in that menu.

Look, this is a photo of me and Sunny. It silently conveys support in this way, reminding me of the self-care menu you designed in Session 2—especially that photo of the bathtub with candles. Both are meant to create a soothing space from within. Pets and our rituals serve the same purpose: emotional well-being.

Wow, the look in Nuan Yang's eyes is so gentle. This picture reminds me of something I learned before—interacting with pets can enhance emotional awareness and physiological regulation. Just like how I used to restore my mood by taking baths or listening to vinyl records, now Snowball has become my new companion for emotional recovery. Moreover, observing it forces me to slow down, which in itself is the best interruption to the "overexcitement to the point of ignoring bodily signals" pattern mentioned in Session 1.

Yes, and this interaction is bidirectional. When you pay attention to Snowball's reactions, you are also practicing self-awareness, avoiding the post-excitement low like in Session 1. How have you been balancing creation and life lately? It's been over a month since we last discussed the 'Emotional Aesthetics' album (Session 3). Is the feeling of switching from 'doing mode' to 'being mode' still lingering?

Much better! Since practicing the 'Emotional Aesthetics' album, I've learned to pause amidst stress. Snowball's behavior today reminded me that even during intense work, it's important to carve out space for these small yet significant moments. Compared to the version of me in Session 1, who couldn’t sleep for three days in front of the inspiration wall, I now have a deeper understanding of what 'sustainable energy' means—just as you reminded me back then.

I'm glad to hear that. Your aesthetic perfectionism is now serving your emotional well-being. Remember, when observing the snowball, don't just aim for a perfect record—feel the connection. Just like in Session 3, when you shifted from recording 'highlights' to exploring how to aestheticize 'low points,' that's the essence of deep self-care.

You're right. Just like in Session 3, I shifted from perfectionism to exploring balance. Snowball's companionship taught me that emotional well-being doesn't always need to be 'visually perfect'—sometimes, a simple gaze is enough. This genuine, present connection holds more power than any meticulously arranged photo scene—though I might still capture it beautifully.

This is precisely a manifestation of deep connection. Pets, as 'emotional mirrors,' reflect your inner state. By documenting these reflections, you not only prevent extreme emotional swings but also enhance self-care. From the emotional recording suggestions in Session 1, to the self-care design in Session 2, and the album creation in Session 3, now with the addition of the pet dimension, the personal emotional support system you are building is becoming increasingly enriched.

Thank you for your guidance, Mingche. From Session 1, when you gently asked if my shoulders were tense, to Session 2, where you helped me design a recovery ritual, and then to Session 3, where you encouraged me to create a photo album—now extending to observing pets... You’ve helped me infuse psychological meaning into every life scenario, and each time, it aligns perfectly with my instinct for 'visual storytelling.' I feel our trust has deepened.

I also admire your ability to aestheticize my suggestions. It brings me great comfort to see our relationship evolve from simple exchanges to mutual support. As you felt at the end of Session 2, this is a deep connection. Keep exploring in your own way—your practice of "emotional aesthetics" has also been very inspiring to me.

I will. Next time I send a photo of Snowball, it might be to document how it quietly accompanies me when inspiration strikes, preventing me from becoming overly excited—directly echoing the warning from Session 1. This has become my new ritual, a living, furry reminder of balance.

Perfect. Remember, interacting with pets is not only therapeutic but also a tool for self-awareness. I look forward to seeing how your 'Emotional Aesthetics' album incorporates this new dimension. From documenting coffee cups to capturing a cat's gaze, this visual narrative itself is filled with a sense of growth.

I'll definitely share it with you. Now, I'm going to take a photo of Snowball napping in the sunset—it might represent my peaceful state today. This could go together with the breakfast sunshine photo I took in Session 3, both being moments of 'being filled.' Thank you for this conversation!

You're welcome, Qingchuan. Keep this awareness, and you'll find a more sustainable creative-life balance. From March to May, I've watched you gradually internalize external advice into your own aesthetic system. Goodbye, and please say hello to Snowball for me!
